name: Cordyceps
short: Case reports: a liver vessel disorder, prolonged bleeding after dental surgery, lead poisoning from tainted powder. Most kidney-transplant trials left adverse events unmonitored or poorly documented.
text: Trial evidence on safety is thin: a systematic review of nine randomised trials of Cordyceps sinensis added to immunosuppressant treatment in kidney transplant patients found that adverse events were either not monitored or poorly documented in most trials; in the four trials comparing cordyceps-based with azathioprine-based treatment, the cordyceps groups had lower rates of high uric acid, high blood lipids, high blood sugar and liver injury. Reports of harm are individual case reports. One describes a patient who took Cordyceps sinensis daily and had prolonged bleeding after dental surgery. Another describes an 81-year-old woman with hepatoportal sclerosis (a disorder of the small veins of the liver) that the authors attributed to Cordyceps after excluding other causes and that improved when she stopped it. A third describes two people with lead poisoning from Cordyceps powder contaminated with lead, which is a contamination problem rather than an effect of the fungus itself. In the transplant trials cordyceps was combined with immunosuppressants, and the review reports that the group given cordyceps with cyclosporine A showed less treatment-induced kidney toxicity than the group given cyclosporine A alone; the abstract does not describe this as a drug interaction. No interaction data were found in the cited sources.
